who does it within the organization and from how the business achieves value from that activity.

2.1 Defining a Business Capability 
Defining a business capability involves identifying and describing what needs to be done by the 
business in support of its overall mission. A business capability description does not imply how 
well something needs to be done, simply that it needs to exist. The following guidelines explain 
how to define an individual business capability.

Naming the business capability is the first step in the capability definition process. It establishes

2.1.1 Naming Convention 
Naming the business capability is the first step in the capability definition process. It establishes 
a  clear  need  for  the  existence  of  the  business  capability  and  helps  to  ensure  it  is  clearly 
distinguishable from other business capabilities. 
The  naming  convention  involves  expressing  the  business  capability  in  a  noun-verb  format, 
whereby  each  outcome  (input,  output,  or  deliverable)  is  described  as  a  noun  and  each  activity 
that is associated with producing or controlling or monitoring the outcome is described as a verb; 
e.g., “Project Management” or “Strategy Planning”. The noun part of the business capability is a 
unique  business  object – a  single,  persistent  thing  that  is  of  interest  to  the  business.  The 
advantage  of  making  a  business  object  the  focal  point  of  the  business  capability  is  that  it

advantage  of  making  a  business  object  the  focal  point  of  the  business  capability  is  that  it 
simplifies  the  process  of  identifying the  information  objects  that  are  tied  to  and  used  by  the 
business capability. 
A business object is typically tangible – for example, “Customer” or “Loan” – but it can also be 
more conceptual and intangible, such as “Research”. The most important consideration is to use 
names  that  resonate  with  business  leaders  and  stakeholders.  Commonly  understood  names

3 Business Capability Mapping 
A business capability map represents the complete, stable set of business capabilities (along with 
all of their defining characteristics) that covers the business, enterprise, or organizational unit in 
question. The end-product of the modeling process is typically a business capability map, which 
provides the visual depiction (or blueprint) of all the business capabilities at an appropriate level 
of decomposition, logically grouped into different categories or perspectives to enable effective 
analysis and planning. 
Once defined, the business capability map provides a self-contained view of the business that is 
independent   of   the   current   organizational   structure,   business   processes,   IT   systems   and 
applications,  and  the  product  or  service  portfolio.  However,  mapping  the  business  capabilities

plans will provide greater insight into the alignment and optimization of each of those domains.

3.2.1 Business Capability Stratification 
Stratification is  the  process  of  classifying,  grouping,  and  aligning  business  capabilities  within

map so that it can be more easily understood; a collection of 20 to 30 capabilities without some 
form of stratification is difficult to read and process. 
Each  stratification  tier provides  a  different  perspective  or  focal  point  for  different  stakeholder 
groups,  allowing each  group to  organize  their  analysis  and  subsequent  planning  activities  in

6.1 Integration of C-MDM Systems 
6.1.1 C-MDM Integration Styles 
The three main C-MDM integration styles are: consolidation, cooperation, and centralized. They 
are described below. 
These three styles are not mutually-exclusive and can be used in combination. If the organization 
has not started their IT journey with the centralized style, it will have to start with consolidation 
and evolve toward cooperation. 
Consolidation Style (or Downstream MDM) 
All  systems  have  their  own  data.  Updates  are  pushed  to  the  MDM  hub  where  they  are 
consolidated. This is the simplest to implement because it has no impact on operational systems. 
It  is  the  first  step for organizations  starting  with the C-MDM capability. The BI & Analytics 
capability  can  be  a simple solution  here.  It  addresses  the  need for after-the-fact analyses  and

capability  can  be  a simple solution  here.  It  addresses  the  need for after-the-fact analyses  and 
reporting  that  require  customer  data.  Nevertheless,  as  there  is  no  single  point  of  truth  for  the 
customer and no impact on operational processes, data  quality will be difficult to improve, and 
merge will not be possible. 
Cooperation Style 
All  systems  have  their  own  data.  Updates  are  pushed  to  the  MDM  hub  where  they  are 
consolidated. The “new version of the truth” is then forwarded to all connected systems that can 
synchronize with the master through the customer ID attributed by the C-MDM application. The 
cooperation style is more complex from an IT point of view, but it allows a high level of control 
on customer data quality and governance in information systems that have been built in silos. In 
this style, the  MDM  capability  is  supporting  user  interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  to

on customer data quality and governance in information systems that have been built in silos. In 
this style, the  MDM  capability  is  supporting  user  interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  to 
create,  update,  merge, or  delete  customer  data  that  cannot  be  addressed  by  BI & Analytics 
platforms. A specific transactional application is therefore required. 
Centralized Style 
No  system  has its own  data.  The  MDM  is  the  only  system  that  stores  the  master  data.  All 
connected  systems  retrieve  the  master  data  from  the  MDM:  identifying  the  customer  with  the 
same  data and when creating a  new customer and checking capability if it already exists in the 
repository.  In  the  same  way as the cooperation  style, this MDM  capability  must  support  user 
interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  and  will  be  supported  by  a  specific  transactional 
application.

1 Introduction 
1.1 Context 
The  modern Digital  Enterprise faces  multiple  challenges  in  its  transformation  to  the  digital 
economy.  New  technologies – cloud, Internet  of  Things  (IoT),  Machine  Learning (ML), 
Artificial  Intelligence (AI) – and  new  techniques – organizational  agility,  continuous  delivery, 
DevOps, etc. – both demand attention. 
To cope with this fast technology evolution pace and succeed in this digital ecosystem, changes 
should  be  pervasive  through  the  whole  organization. Digital Transformation as strategy  should 
be  aligned  with  the  overall  organization  context  and  environment  and  should  be  derived  and 
sometimes  even  replace  the  existing  organization  strategy.  The  new  digital  capabilities  thus 
become essential outcomes for an effective Digital Transformation program.

2 The History of Capability-Based Planning 
Capability-based planning was introduced by the Research and Technology Organization (RTO) 
Studies,   Analysis, and   Simulation   (SAS)   panel   for   NATO.   Multiple   nations’ military 
organizations needed the ability to jointly plan based on scenarios of expected future operations. 
“(The) ... description  of  the  task  force  structure  units  should  be  able  to  perform  expressed  in 
capability  terms.  Once  the  capability  inventory  is  defined,  the  most cost-effective  and  efficient 
physical force unit options to implement these capabilities are derived.” (Source: Handbook on 
Long-Term Defence Planning; see Referenced Documents) 
The  recommendation  made  by  the  military  planners  was  to  move  away  from  threat-based 
planning  and  explore  several  potential  scenarios.  Capabilities  and capability  “segments” are

The  recommendation  made  by  the  military  planners  was  to  move  away  from  threat-based 
planning  and  explore  several  potential  scenarios.  Capabilities  and capability  “segments” are 
mapped against multiple scenarios to see how well the capabilities fulfill the objectives of each 
scenario. This assessment then supports which  capabilities need investment over time  based  on 
the ones that allowed the response to the most scenarios.

5.1 Value Streams in Business Capability Planning 
The  approach  to  value  analysis  that  is  used  in Business  Architecture  is  derived  from “Great 
Transition” by  James  Martin  (see Referenced  Documents). The  value  stream is  depicted  as  an 
end-to-end  collection  of  value-adding  activities  that  create  an  overall  result  for  a  customer, 
stakeholder,  or  end  user. In  modeling  terms,  those  value-adding  activities  are  represented  by 
value  stream  stages,  each  of  which  creates  and  adds  incremental  stakeholder  value  from  one 
stage to the next. 
Value   streams   may   be   externally   triggered,   such   as   a   retail   customer   acquiring   some 
merchandise as  shown  in  the  example  below.  Value  streams  may  also  be  internally  triggered, 
such  as  a  manager  obtaining  a  new  hire as  shown  above.  Value  streams  may  be  defined  at  an

such  as  a  manager  obtaining  a  new  hire as  shown  above.  Value  streams  may  be  defined  at  an 
enterprise level or at a business unit level. Either way, the complete set of value streams denotes 
an organization’s primary set of business activities. It is an aggregation of the multiple ways in 
which the enterprise creates value for its various stakeholders. 
A  key  principle  of  value  streams  is  that  value  is  always  defined  from  the  perspective  of  the 
stakeholder – the customer, end user, or recipient of the product, service, or deliverable produced 
by  the  work.  The  value  obtained  is  in  the  eye  of  the  beholder;  it  depends  more  on  the 
stakeholder’s perception of the worth of the product, service, outcome, or deliverable than on its 
intrinsic value; i.e., the cost to produce.

7.3 Digital Transformation and Business Capability Planning 
Digital  Transformation is   held   at  times  to  be  a   specialized   form   of  innovation  that  is 
disproportionate to other forms  of innovation. This perception is due to many factors including

fear of change that hinders the adoption of most innovation. 
Business capability planning has the potential to make Digital Transformation less daunting and

create  new  business  capability  instances  that  are  combined  with  existing  business  capability 
instances  that  can  be  more  rapidly  implemented.  When  put  in  the  light  of  value  streams  and

3 Metadata Management Capability 
Simplistically, metadata can be called “data about data”. For example, metadata indicates who is 
the  author/creator  of  the  data,  when  it  was  created,  its  security  classification,  its  data  quality 
attributes, and  so  on.  According  to  the Data  Management  Body  of  Knowledge  (DMBOK2), 
pp.417 – see Referenced Documents: 
“Metadata helps  an  organization  understand  its  data,  its  systems,  and  its  workflows.  It  enables 
quality  assessment and  is  integral  to  the  management  of  databases and  other  applications.  It 
contributes to the ability to process, maintain, integrate, secure, audit, and govern other data.” 
The  concept  of  metadata  is  not  new  and  is  widely  used in  the  IT  industry  to  define  data  about 
data. In  ancient  times  long  before  the  digital  age,  metadata  such  as  author,  title,  number  of

data. In  ancient  times  long  before  the  digital  age,  metadata  such  as  author,  title,  number  of 
tablets,  etc. was already  used to  catalog  collections of  clay tablets.  As  such,  metadata  provides 
additional information to better know and use the data. 
Metadata Management is the planning, implementation, and control activity that enables access 
to  high-quality,  integrated  metadata (Source: DMBOK2,  pp.419).  It  enhances  the  data  with 
additional information so that it can be used to: 
 Know your data: 
— Reduce uncertainty and possible misinterpretation of the data 
— Know the quality of the data available and associated business rules (data quality 
business rules, transformation business rules, etc.) 
— Data origin and usage of the data 
— Improve auditing of Business Intelligence (BI) reports 
— Monitor data volume across the information system to reduce environmental impact 
 Manage the data risk and compliance with regulatory requirements:

— Monitor data volume across the information system to reduce environmental impact

— Leverage security and privacy metadata for the enterprise’s most valuable asset; for

— Security metadata enables the transition from network-centric to attribute-centric

— Enterprise identity management relies on a federated identity (common

— Privacy legislation in many countries and/or groups of countries (e.g., the

Metadata is all too often delegated to IT, whereas it is essentially a business concern. Subsequent 
to numerous investigations in the mid-2000s and new government legislation, metadata is a key 
corporate asset that has to be maintained to ensure shareholder transparency, corporate security, 
and client privacy. 
The rise of  NoSQL databases  (relaxed  data  schemas)  and  the  recent  big  data trends  with  the 
associated promise to unlock value  from any kind of data, have led  to focus solely on building 
the  capabilities  to  collect,  store, and  analyze  the  data.  Very  little  effort  was  put  on  metadata 
which  is  often  depicted  as  irrelevant  or  available  automatically  using  machine  learning  tools. 
Beyond  market  trends,  Metadata  Management  is  still  a  challenge  in  many  organizations  for

Beyond  market  trends,  Metadata  Management  is  still  a  challenge  in  many  organizations  for 
multiple reasons: 
 IT complexity: 
— Legacy applications are poorly documented: reference data is lacking, and data 
changes its meaning during the lifecycle of the application 
— Mergers and acquisitions are increasing the IT landscape and therefore the scope of 
metadata to be documented is changing 
— The replication factor: this concept defines how many times a data element (e.g., 
customer first name) is replicated in the information system; the higher the replication 
factor, the more challenging the metadata documentation effort 
 Data complexity: 
— Variety and velocity of data collected (e.g., social media feeds or logs collected near 
real-time, text and image collected for machine learning purpose, etc.) require new 
techniques to collect the relevant metadata

 IT marketing trends: 
— Microservices/micro applications often challenge data lineage and increase the

— “Agile” delivery is incorrectly interpreted as no requirement for documentation 
 Manual work: 
— How to capture the information with business and IT Small and Medium Enterprises

— What is the right granularity and priority criteria? 
— Metadata validation is not automatic and needs a human review 
 Lack of data standards: 
— Naming conventions

understanding  of  the  data  already  available  within  the  organization. Therefore,  metadata  is  an 
important  foundational  data management  capacity  for  any  organization  looking  to efficiently

 Operational metadata describes details of the processing and accessing of data

Looking back at the history of BI & Analytics on the market, different architecture pattern styles 
and technical solutions  have  been  used. For a given  organization, the coexistence  of several BI 
& Analytics capabilities using different technologies and duplicating data comes with difficulties 
if the following principles quoted in the TOGAF Standard [C220] are not respected: 
• Principle 11: Data is Shared 
Users have access to the data necessary to perform their duties; therefore, data is shared 
across enterprise functions and organizations (...) It is less costly to maintain timely, 
accurate data in a single application, and then share it, than it is to maintain duplicative 
data in multiple applications. 
For a given Organization Information System having the data kept first in an “Infocenter”

data in multiple applications. 
For a given Organization Information System having the data kept first in an “Infocenter” 
and then copied in a “data warehouse” for other analytics is costly and complex. 
• Principle 20: Control Technical Diversity 
Technological diversity is controlled to minimize the non-trivial cost of maintaining 
expertise in and connectivity between multiple processing environments. 
For a given Organization Information System maintaining both data warehouse running 
on Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) and Data Lake on Hadoop

comes with IT cost and complexity that should be justified with business value.

for the BI & Analytics, the replacement of the legacy architecture by the new one is performed.

historical  data  to  understand  past  events  and  trends,

or  trends observed in the descriptive stage, Predictive

identified trends, and Prescriptive aims to recommend or 
automate.

the defined use cases ultimately lead to specific actions 
within the company.

Incorporating AI Governance Practices to Mitigate Risks: 
The incorporation of AI governance practices into the AI 
framework is crucial for overcoming various risks associated 
with  bias,  model  drift,  and  data  quality  degradation.  The 
sources  highlighted  that  AI  governance  focuses  on

establishing  a  robust  structure,  processes,  and  controls  to 
ensure the responsible and ethical use of AI throughout its 
lifecycle  [45][46]  to  address  Bias  (Data  Quality 
Management, Fairness), Bias Mitigation, and Equal Access. 
For  Transparency  and  Accountability:  AI  governance 
promotes transparency by requiring clear documentation and 
communication about the AI system's purpose, functionality, 
and limitations. This enables potential sources of bias as well 
as responsibly and ethically usage. 
For  combating  Model  Drift,  there  are  steps  like 
Continuous  Improvement,  Testing  and  Review  Processes, 
Model Testing and Validation, and Compliance Checks.

steward may be broader and include data standardization and definition tasks.

Data Governance Overview
Data Governance is how an enterprise manages its data assets. Governance includes the rules, 
policies, procedures, roles and responsibilities that guide overall management of an enterprise’s data.
▪Accountability for the management of data assets.  Data Stewards do 
not own the data; instead they are the caretakers of the enterprise data 
assets.  The Data Stewards ensure the quality, accuracy and security of 
the data.

utilizes to manage its data assets.  Data Policies might include 
adherence  of data to business rules, enforcing authentication and 
access rights to data, compliance with laws and regulations, and 
protection of data assets.

The technology visioning process to align IT capabilities with 
business needs typically involves the following steps:
Assess Current State: Evaluate the existing IT infrastructure, systems, and capabilities to 
understand the current state of technology within the organization.
Understand Business Objectives: Closely collaborate with business leaders to identify the 
organization's strategic goals, objectives, and priorities. Understand the key business drivers, 
challenges, and pain points.
Identify Technology Trends: Research and analyze the emerging technology trends, 
innovations, and best practices that can potentially benefit the organization and support its 
business goals.
Conduct Gap Analysis: Compare the current IT capabilities with the identified business 
needs and technology trends to determine the gaps and areas for improvement.

The technology visioning process is an iterative and collaborative effort that requires 
close coordination between the IT team and the business to ensure that the 
organization's technology capabilities are closely aligned with its strategic objectives 
and priorities.
Define the Technology Vision: Based on the assessment, business objectives, and identified gaps, develop a 
comprehensive technology vision that aligns IT capabilities with the organization's long-term strategic 
direction.
Establish Technology Roadmap: Outline a detailed roadmap that outlines the specific technology initiatives, 
investments, and milestones required to realize the technology vision. This roadmap should include 
timelines, resource requirements, and dependencies.
Prioritize Initiatives: Prioritize the technology initiatives based on their potential impact, alignment with 
business needs, feasibility, and available resources.

operating models, and economic opportunities.

combustion engine, which conquered physical distance. Following this, we will analyze the Internet, the digital network that facilitated global connection 
and dematerialized commerce. Finally, we will apply this historical framework to the ongoing revolution in Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises an 
era of mass cognition.

The public and corporate debate often frames the impact of AI in a simplistic binary: will it "replace" or "augment" human jobs? History suggests this is a false

knowledge-work role by automating certain tasks within that role. This will force a redefinition of the human's value proposition.

task automated by AI) and more time on system architecture and

Shifting from "How" to "What" and "Why"
As AI tools become increasingly proficient at the "how" of a task—how to

premium on human skill will migrate to the "what" and the "why."

The future of work will belong not to those who can simply execute tasks, but to those who can wisely direct the powerful new tools of cognition.

model is characterized by the hyper-automation of processes, the embedding of predictive intelligence into all decision-making, and the 
fundamental reorganization of work around human-AI collaboration.

AI enables a new, deeper level of automation that moves beyond simple, discrete tasks to encompass entire end-to-end business workflows. This 
"intelligent automation" is being applied across the enterprise. In human resources, AI-driven systems can handle routine employee inquiries, 
manage payroll, and track performance, freeing HR professionals to focus on strategic talent management. In finance, AI can automate data entry

AI and machine learning models can analyze vast streams of real-time 
and historical data to forecast future outcomes with increasing accuracy.

them. For example, predictive maintenance in manufacturing can

next evolutionary step is prescriptive analytics, where AI systems will not

"offer customer X a specific, personalized discount to maximize retention 
probability").

Norm
The dominant operating model of the future will be one of human-AI collaboration. In this model, AI is not just a back-office automation tool but a "digital

assigned and measured.

management. In a competitive landscape where some leaders have access to AI-driven insights, decisions based purely on 
"gut feeling" or past experience will become a significant liability.
A manager relying on intuition is competing against a manager armed with a superhuman analytical tool capable of 
processing information at a scale and speed no human can match. Over time, the data-driven approach will consistently 
outperform, making it a competitive necessity. The operating model of the future must therefore embed AI-driven analytics

In the AI economy, competitive advantage will increasingly be derived 
from proprietary data and the superior AI models trained on that data. 
This creates a powerful new competitive "moat." A company with a

virtuous cycle or "data flywheel" that can lead to formidable, defensible 
market leadership.

AI Ethics as a Strategic Imperative
Finally, as AI becomes deeply embedded in every product, service, and decision, the ethical implications of its use—issues of bias, fairness, 
transparency, and privacy—move from being a peripheral compliance concern to a central business risk and strategic imperative. A biased AI model 
used for hiring or loan approvals can trigger a massive legal, financial, and reputational crisis. This risk is so fundamental that it cannot be delegated 
to a mid-level IT or legal team.
Critical Business Risk
The governance of AI must become a board-level strategic conversation. This will necessitate the rise of a new C-suite function, a Chief 
Ethics Officer or equivalent, responsible for ensuring AI is developed and deployed responsibly. A company's brand, its customer trust, and 
its very business model will become inextricably linked to its ethical framework for AI.

Synthesis and Strategic 
Imperatives
The preceding analysis of five major technological revolutions—the Printing Press, 
the Steam Engine, the Age of Mobility, the Internet, and Artificial Intelligence—reveals 
a consistent and powerful blueprint of change. Despite the vast differences in the 
technologies themselves, the pattern of their impact on the business landscape has 
been remarkably stable. This section synthesizes the findings from the case studies to 
distill these enduring patterns of disruption and, based on them, provides a set of 
actionable strategic imperatives for leaders navigating the current AI-driven 
transformation.

understanding the likely trajectory of the AI revolution.

The invention of the movable-type printing press by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440 was not merely an improvement on writing; it was the first

altered the economic, social, and intellectual fabric of Europe, providing a pristine historical case study that perfectly illustrates the three-pronged

The steam engine and the machinery it powered were incompatible with the small-scale, distributed cottage industry. This technological shift necessitated a new operating

The defining characteristic of the factory system was the centralization of 
production in a single, large-scale facility. This was an economic and technical 
necessity. The new machines were too large, too expensive, and too power-hungry 
to be housed in a worker's cottage. They required a central power source—a water 
wheel or, more flexibly, a steam engine—to drive the shafts and belts that powered

small part of the overall process. This specialization dramatically increased the 
speed and efficiency of production, boosting output per worker and lowering the 
cost of goods.

The factory system was built on the principle of standardization. Using machinery

popularized by inventors like Eli Whitney. This machine-driven precision, overseen

provided the immense capital required to build and equip the factory. A new 
professional middle class of managers, engineers, and supervisors was created to 
design the products, manage the operations, and oversee the workforce. The vast

The factory system can be understood as more than just a new way to organize people; it was a physical manifestation of an algorithm for production. It took a complex craft, 
such as making cloth or building a musket, and deconstructed it into a sequence of simple, repeatable steps that could be executed in a precise order by a combination of 
human and mechanical components. This "proceduralization" of work—codifying it into a repeatable, scalable, and optimized process—is the core logic of industrial 
efficiency. It is also the direct conceptual ancestor of the computer program, which applies the same logic of sequential, rule-based execution to information-based tasks, 
and of modern business process management.

that of women and children, dangerous working conditions, and severe environmental pollution in the new industrial cities. These negative externalities were not 
accidental side effects but direct consequences of the model's logic. This created a fundamental tension between capital and labor that would define political and 
social conflict for the next 150 years, leading to the rise of powerful labor unions, the emergence of socialist political movements, and eventually, the creation of

New Business Models and Economic Opportunities
The immense scale of production and capital required by the factory system could not be supported by traditional business structures like partnerships or sole 
proprietorships. This pressure gave rise to new legal and financial business models that were capable of aggregating and deploying capital on an unprecedented scale, 
creating the foundations of modern industrial capitalism.

The Modern Corporation and Financial 
Innovation
The Modern Corporation
The signature business model of the industrial era was the modern corporation, a new legal and 
financial structure that evolved to meet the demands of large-scale industry. Industries like 
railroads and steel required massive, long-term capital investments that were far beyond the 
means of a few individuals. The corporation solved this problem through several key 
innovations:
Separate Legal Personality
A corporation was recognized as a legal entity separate and distinct from its owners. This 
allowed it to own assets, enter into contracts, and incur liabilities in its own name.
Limited Liability
This was the most critical feature. It protected the corporation's owners (the shareholders) 
from being held personally responsible for the company's debts beyond the amount of their 
individual investment. This legal shield dramatically reduced the risk for investors and

Capital Accumulation through Shares
The corporation could raise enormous sums of capital by selling ownership shares (stock) to 
a wide and dispersed pool of public investors. This provided the financing necessary for 
building factories, transcontinental railroads, and other massive industrial projects.
New Financial Institutions and Markets
The voracious capital demands of industry also spurred a revolution in the financial sector. A 
sophisticated ecosystem of banks and financial markets developed to channel savings into 
industrial investment.
Industrial Banking
The banking system expanded and specialized to serve industrial clients. A network of

Industrial Banking
The banking system expanded and specialized to serve industrial clients. A network of 
private and county banks, and later powerful joint-stock banks, emerged to provide the 
short-term circulating capital and long-term loans that entrepreneurs needed. These banks 
played a crucial role in channeling funds from capital-rich agricultural regions to the new, 
capital-hungry industrial centers. Historical analysis shows that the establishment of stable 
national banks in the U.S. after the Civil War was a major determinant of the subsequent 
geographic distribution of manufacturing, as these banks provided the necessary financing 
for firms to invest in capital and steam power.

markets, where corporate shares could be bought and sold, grew in importance, providing 
liquidity for investors and a mechanism for valuing these large new enterprises.

The Age of Mobility - The Internal Combustion Engine 
and the Conquest of Distance
Following the age of steam, the next great technological wave was defined by the perfection and proliferation of the internal combustion engine 
(ICE). This was the technology that truly conquered distance, untethering power from the factory and the railway and putting it into the hands of 
individuals. The automobile and the airplane, the prime applications of the ICE, did not just make travel faster; they fundamentally re-architected the 
physical landscape of nations, created a new culture of personal freedom, and gave rise to some of the 20th century's largest industries.

The Internal Combustion Engine (ICE)

inefficient. The ICE, perfected in the late 19th century by 
inventors like Karl Benz, offered a far superior

transport, bringing with it a multitude of benefits and 
problems, including environmental pollution from the 
burning of fossil fuels.
The Automobile
Initially a hand-built luxury item for the wealthy, the 
automobile was transformed into a mass-market product by 
Henry Ford. The Ford Model T, introduced in 1908, was 
designed to be durable, simple to operate, and, most 
importantly, affordable. It was a "universal car" that used 
innovations like a single-cast engine block and lightweight 
vanadium steel to serve the needs of a nation.

New Business Models and Economic Opportunities: A Nation on Wheels
The automobile and the airplane did not just create new products; they created entirely new economies, transforming consumer behavior, finance, and the American landscape.
Mass-Market Consumerism and Credit
The automobile was the quintessential 20th-century consumer durable. 
Henry Ford's business model was revolutionary: he deliberately lowered 
the price of the Model T to expand the market, correctly believing that 
volume would lead to profits. This created a new paradigm of 
mass-market consumerism.
However, even at $300, a car was a major purchase. This gave rise to 
another critical business model innovation: widespread consumer credit. 
To compete with the low cash price of the Model T, other manufacturers 
began offering installment sales plans. By 1925, roughly three-quarters 
of all new cars were bought "on time," establishing the habit of 
purchasing expensive goods on credit as a pillar of the American

of all new cars were bought "on time," establishing the habit of 
purchasing expensive goods on credit as a pillar of the American 
middle-class economy.
The Automotive Ecosystem
The proliferation of the automobile created a vast ecosystem of new 
industries and jobs, reshaping the economy and the physical country.
•Spin-off Industries: Demand for steel, rubber, petroleum, and glass 
skyrocketed.
•New Service Businesses: A whole new landscape of roadside 
businesses emerged to serve the needs of motorists. This included 
gas stations, mechanic repair shops, motels, and diners.
•Infrastructure and Suburbanization: The "Good Roads" movement, 
fueled by political pressure from new motorists, led to massive 
government investment in paving roads and building highways. This 
new infrastructure, in turn, enabled the rise of the suburbs, as 
people could now live far from their city jobs and commute by car.

The Birth of Commercial Aviation
The airline industry itself represented a completely new business model. 
Early pioneers demonstrated the technical possibility of flight, but 
creating a scheduled, reliable service was a business challenge. Early 
airlines like DELAG in Germany (using airships) and the St. 
Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line in the U.S. were the first to offer scheduled 
service. While initially dependent on mail subsidies, these companies laid 
the groundwork for a global passenger and cargo network. The 
development of larger and more reliable aircraft like the Douglas DC-3 
eventually made passenger travel profitable on its own, fueling the growth 
of international tourism and global business and connecting the world in a 
way that was previously unimaginable.

The Digital Revolution - The Network of Global Connection
The third great technological wave, the Digital Revolution, was catalyzed by the convergence of the personal computer and the internet. This created a global, ubiquitous network that 
dematerialized commerce, communication, and work, ushering in an information-based economy. The internet's impact provides a clear, modern illustration of the three-pronged framework, 
demonstrating how a general-purpose technology for communication and computation can reshape the business world.
Technology, Tools, and Skills: From Analog to Digital
The Digital Revolution was built upon a stack of interconnected technologies that replaced analog tools with digital equivalents, demanding a new form of literacy and a host of new specialized 
skills from the global workforce.

making the internet a constant and portable presence.

protocols that allowed disparate computer networks to

Built atop this infrastructure, a vast ecosystem of new

The New Skillset of the Knowledge Worker and Digital Business Models
The New Skillset of the Knowledge Worker
The shift to a digital economy rendered many clerical and analog skills obsolete and created a demand for a new set of cognitive 
and technical abilities.
Digital Literacy
At the most basic level, digital literacy—the ability to confidently use computers, navigate the internet, and operate common 
software applications—became a fundamental prerequisite for participation in the modern workforce. This extended beyond 
mere technical operation to include higher-order skills like critically evaluating the credibility of online information and 
understanding the basics of cybersecurity.
Specialized Technical Skills
The new digital economy created immense demand for a new class of technical professionals. Businesses required workers 
with advanced skills in areas such as web development, network administration, cybersecurity, and database management. As

with advanced skills in areas such as web development, network administration, cybersecurity, and database management. As 
businesses moved online, new marketing disciplines emerged, creating jobs for specialists in Search Engine Optimization 
(SEO) and Search Engine Marketing (SEM) who could help companies become visible and attract customers in the crowded 
digital marketplace. Data analytics also became a critical skill, as businesses sought to make sense of the vast amounts of user 
data they were now able to collect.
Soft Skills and Digital Intelligence (DQ)
Beyond purely technical skills, the new environment demanded what has been termed "Digital Intelligence" or DQ. This is a set 
of social, emotional, and cognitive abilities necessary for navigating online life effectively and ethically. These competencies 
include managing one's digital identity and reputation, engaging in effective digital communication and collaboration, and

include managing one's digital identity and reputation, engaging in effective digital communication and collaboration, and

New Business Models and Economic Opportunities
The unique technical and economic properties of the internet—global reach, zero marginal cost of distribution for digital goods, 
and the ability to facilitate communication at scale—gave rise to a host of entirely new business models that have come to define 
the modern economy.
Software as a Service (SaaS)
The SaaS model fundamentally disrupted the traditional software industry. Instead of selling a perpetual license for a piece of 
software that the customer would install on their own premises (on-premise), SaaS vendors offered their software as a service, 
hosted in the cloud and accessed via a web browser. This model dramatically lowered the barrier to entry for customers and

hosted in the cloud and accessed via a web browser. This model dramatically lowered the barrier to entry for customers and 
provided vendors with stable, recurring revenue streams.
Platform Business Models
Perhaps the most powerful business model enabled by the internet is the platform. A platform does not create value by 
producing and selling a good or service itself; rather, it creates value by facilitating exchanges and interactions between two or 
more distinct user groups, such as producers and consumers. Examples include marketplaces like Amazon and eBay, social 
media networks like Facebook, and service platforms like Uber. These businesses leverage network effects, becoming more 
valuable to each user as more users join.

The Subscription and Freemium Economy
Beyond SaaS, the internet popularized subscription and freemium models across many industries. Companies like Netflix and 
Spotify applied the recurring revenue model to media and entertainment, shifting from ownership of individual items to 
access to vast libraries of content for a flat monthly fee. The freemium model offers basic services for free to attract users, 
then converts a percentage to paying customers who upgrade to premium features.
A fundamental distinction of the Digital Revolution was the "democratization" of the tools of production. Unlike the printing press or the steam engine, which were massive capital goods, the core tools of the digital era—software and information—have a marginal cost

of reproduction that is effectively zero. This dramatically lowered the barriers to entry for entrepreneurship. An individual or small team could now access world-class tools (open-source software, pay-as-you-go cloud computing) and reach a global market instantly via 
the internet, all with minimal upfront capital investment. This economic reality, described as the internet's role as a "great leveler," made it possible for a small firm to be a "global company from day one," fueling the explosion of startups and "micro-multinationals" that 
has defined the last three decades.

The AI Revolution - The Dawn of Mass Cognition and Strategic Imperatives
The fourth and current technological transformation is being driven by Artificial Intelligence. This report posits that AI is a general-purpose technology for automating and augmenting cognitive work, just as the steam engine automated and augmented manual work. 
While still in its early stages, the AI revolution is already beginning to demonstrate the classic three-pronged impact on business, reshaping tools, skills, operating models, and economic opportunities.
Synthesis and Strategic Imperatives
The preceding analysis of five major technological revolutions—the Printing Press, the Steam Engine, the Age of Mobility, the Internet, and Artificial Intelligence—reveals a consistent and powerful blueprint of change. Despite the vast differences in the technologies 
themselves, the pattern of their impact on the business landscape has been remarkably stable.

Anticipate the Skill Shift: Focus on Tasks, Not Jobs
History teaches that focusing on which job titles will be eliminated is the wrong approach. Leaders must instead deconstruct roles into their component tasks and analyze which 
are routine and susceptible to automation by AI, and which require uniquely human skills like creativity, critical thinking, strategic judgment, and empathy.
Re-imagine Your Operating Model: Avoid Paving the Cowpath
The most common and costly mistake in any technological transition is to simply layer the new technology onto an old operating model in the hope of achieving 
incremental efficiencies. AI is not just a tool to make the 20th-century office slightly more efficient; it is a catalyst for a fundamentally new way of working.
Innovate the Business Model, Not Just the Product

Innovate the Business Model, Not Just the Product
The greatest and most durable value from a technological revolution is captured not by those who use it to make existing products cheaper, but 
by those who use it to invent entirely new business models. Leaders must ask: What is possible now that was impossible before AI?
Embrace the Long, Slow Ramp of Death
The lesson of the productivity paradox is a call for strategic patience. The full benefits of AI will not materialize in a single quarter 
or fiscal year. It requires a long-term, unwavering strategic commitment to investment, experimentation, organizational learning, 
and the tolerance for failure that is inherent in any true innovation process.
In conclusion, the history of technological change is not a series of disconnected events but a continuous story with a clear plot. By understanding this plot—the recurring, three-pronged impact on skills, operating models, and business models—today's leaders can
move from a reactive posture to one of proactive strategy, transforming the disruptive force of Artificial Intelligence from an existential threat into a generational opportunity.

with enhanced support to assist developing countries to do so. As such, it charts a new course in 
the   global   climate   effort   that   concerns   all   economy   sectors,   including   Information   and 
Communication Technologies (ICT).

Governance is the system through which an organization makes decisions and applies them to reach its 
goals. The decision-making process can be formal, relying on well-defined processes, or informal, relying

Including environmental aspects in the decision-making process requires the use of new indicators,

“systems thinking”.

exploring and developing effective action in complex contexts, enabling systems change. In organizations, 
systems consist of people, structures, and processes that work together to make an organization “healthy” 
or “unhealthy”. (See “Thinking in Systems”, by Donella Meadows [Systems Thinking].)

1 Introduction 
The  Business  Architecture defines  the  business  strategy,  governance,  organization,  business 
information, and key business processes of an Enterprise Architecture. An architecture approach 
determines how to effect change within the appropriate cost, benefit, and risk parameters. 
A challenge to this approach arises due to a lack of consistency in the application of architecture 
standards  used  to  inform Business  Architects  or  those intending  to  develop  a  Business 
Architecture  or  technical  solution  on  the  expected  Architecture  Building  Blocks (ABBs)  for 
governments worldwide. 
The  Government Reference  Model (GRM) gives public  sector organizations  a  common  way to 
view themselves in order to plan and execute effective transformational change.

Looking back at the history of BI & Analytics on the market, different architecture pattern styles 
and technical solutions  have  been  used. For a given  organization, the coexistence  of several BI 
& Analytics capabilities using different technologies and duplicating data comes with difficulties 
if the following principles quoted in the TOGAF Standard [C220] are not respected: 
• Principle 11: Data is Shared 
Users have access to the data necessary to perform their duties; therefore, data is shared 
across enterprise functions and organizations (...) It is less costly to maintain timely, 
accurate data in a single application, and then share it, than it is to maintain duplicative 
data in multiple applications. 
For a given Organization Information System having the data kept first in an “Infocenter”

For a given Organization Information System having the data kept first in an “Infocenter” 
and then copied in a “data warehouse” for other analytics is costly and complex. 
• Principle 20: Control Technical Diversity 
Technological diversity is controlled to minimize the non-trivial cost of maintaining 
expertise in and connectivity between multiple processing environments. 
For a given Organization Information System maintaining both data warehouse running 
on Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) and Data Lake on Hadoop

This  document  describes  an  approach  for  implementing Customer  Master  Data  Management 
(C-MDM).  The  purpose  of  C-MDM in  an  organization is to  increase  the  value  of  customer 
information  shared  across  the  organization.  It  includes  people,  process,  organizations,  and 
systems to manage this information as an asset.

Master Data Management (MDM) 
This capability refers to  processes,  organizations,  people,  and  systems  put  together  to  measure 
and continuously improve the value of master and reference data for an organization. It includes 
business value, data quality, availability, and security. It delivers accurate customer data to use-
cases  that  need  it. It  ensures business  value,  data  quality  (uniformity,  accuracy,  semantic 
consistency,  etc.),  availability,  security,  stewardship, and  customer  data  ownership.  MDM 
delivers control over master data values and identifiers that enable consistent use in line with the 
business-defined data quality requirements. 
 
Master Data 
This is data that constitutes the most definitive, trusted values available to the enterprise and is to 
be  both  shared  and  used  for  the  purposes  of  transactions,  analytics,  and/or  records.  For  semi-

be  both  shared  and  used  for  the  purposes  of  transactions,  analytics,  and/or  records.  For  semi-
structured data, it could be the approved enterprise policy on data lifecycle; for structured data, it 
could be  the  name  and  address  of  a  client.  Technically,  master  data  is  a  consistent  set  of 
identifiers  and  extended  attributes  that  is  the  reference  source  of  information  about  shared 
entities used by the enterprise. Master data values are trusted and can be used with confidence by 
authorized users across the enterprise.

3 C-MDM Capability 
For  a  given  organization, C-MDM refers  to  people,  processes,  organizations, and  systems  put 
together  to  manage  kernel  customer  data as  an  asset. It  includes  business  value,  data  quality,

Kernel   customer   data is all   the   customer   information   shared   across the   organization’s 
departments: 
 Mandatory customer data for the organization to ensure at least minimal customer 
experience (name, surname, address, customer ID, etc.) 
 Transverse and strategic customer data for the organization that should be shared across 
the value chain of the organization (customer type, age, professional activity category, 
etc.) 
 Data often already existing outside the context of interaction with the organization

Kernel  customer  data is  mainly  about  identification  keys,  personal  identification  data,  contact 
data,  preferences and consent data,   and   relationships   data   (relations  between   customers, 
hierarchy, etc.). 
The C-MDM capability  is  composed  of  business  and application  functions.  It  requires well 
organized teams (Business Architecture) and adapted information systems (Information Systems 
Architecture).  One  of  the  challenges  for  the C-MDM capability  is  to  find a subtle  balance to 
allow adjustment  between  automation  (in  data  quality,  de-duplication)  and  manual  processes 
when  the  algorithms  do  not produce certainty.  On  the  one  hand  a  lack  of  automation  can

allow adjustment  between  automation  (in  data  quality,  de-duplication)  and  manual  processes 
when  the  algorithms  do  not produce certainty.  On  the  one  hand  a  lack  of  automation  can 
generate  excessive  manual  workflow, but  on  the  other  hand  the  algorithm  cannot  solve  all  the 
data  quality  issues, and  missing  human  intelligence  and  workforce  to  deal  with  those  cases

6.1 Integration of C-MDM Systems 
6.1.1 C-MDM Integration Styles 
The three main C-MDM integration styles are: consolidation, cooperation, and centralized. They 
are described below. 
These three styles are not mutually-exclusive and can be used in combination. If the organization 
has not started their IT journey with the centralized style, it will have to start with consolidation 
and evolve toward cooperation. 
Consolidation Style (or Downstream MDM) 
All  systems  have  their  own  data.  Updates  are  pushed  to  the  MDM  hub  where  they  are 
consolidated. This is the simplest to implement because it has no impact on operational systems. 
It  is  the  first  step for organizations  starting  with the C-MDM capability. The BI & Analytics 
capability  can  be  a simple solution  here.  It  addresses  the  need for after-the-fact analyses  and

capability  can  be  a simple solution  here.  It  addresses  the  need for after-the-fact analyses  and 
reporting  that  require  customer  data.  Nevertheless,  as  there  is  no  single  point  of  truth  for  the 
customer and no impact on operational processes, data  quality will be difficult to improve, and 
merge will not be possible. 
Cooperation Style 
All  systems  have  their  own  data.  Updates  are  pushed  to  the  MDM  hub  where  they  are 
consolidated. The “new version of the truth” is then forwarded to all connected systems that can 
synchronize with the master through the customer ID attributed by the C-MDM application. The 
cooperation style is more complex from an IT point of view, but it allows a high level of control 
on customer data quality and governance in information systems that have been built in silos. In 
this style, the  MDM  capability  is  supporting  user  interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  to

on customer data quality and governance in information systems that have been built in silos. In 
this style, the  MDM  capability  is  supporting  user  interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  to 
create,  update,  merge, or  delete  customer  data  that  cannot  be  addressed  by  BI & Analytics 
platforms. A specific transactional application is therefore required. 
Centralized Style 
No  system  has its own  data.  The  MDM  is  the  only  system  that  stores  the  master  data.  All 
connected  systems  retrieve  the  master  data  from  the  MDM:  identifying  the  customer  with  the 
same  data and when creating a  new customer and checking capability if it already exists in the 
repository.  In  the  same  way as the cooperation  style, this MDM  capability  must  support  user 
interfaces,  workflows, and transactions  and  will  be  supported  by  a  specific  transactional 
application.

3 Metadata Management Capability 
Simplistically, metadata can be called “data about data”. For example, metadata indicates who is 
the  author/creator  of  the  data,  when  it  was  created,  its  security  classification,  its  data  quality 
attributes, and  so  on.  According  to  the Data  Management  Body  of  Knowledge  (DMBOK2), 
pp.417 – see Referenced Documents: 
“Metadata helps  an  organization  understand  its  data,  its  systems,  and  its  workflows.  It  enables 
quality  assessment and  is  integral  to  the  management  of  databases and  other  applications.  It 
contributes to the ability to process, maintain, integrate, secure, audit, and govern other data.” 
The  concept  of  metadata  is  not  new  and  is  widely  used in  the  IT  industry  to  define  data  about 
data. In  ancient  times  long  before  the  digital  age,  metadata  such  as  author,  title,  number  of

data. In  ancient  times  long  before  the  digital  age,  metadata  such  as  author,  title,  number  of 
tablets,  etc. was already  used to  catalog  collections of  clay tablets.  As  such,  metadata  provides 
additional information to better know and use the data. 
Metadata Management is the planning, implementation, and control activity that enables access 
to  high-quality,  integrated  metadata (Source: DMBOK2,  pp.419).  It  enhances  the  data  with 
additional information so that it can be used to: 
 Know your data:

2 What is an Information Map? 
An  Information  Map is  a collection  of  information  concepts and their  relationships to  one 
another. Information concepts, in effect, reflect the business’ vocabulary; e.g., client, account, or

A.3 Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERDs) 
ERDs have a long history in information systems design. They are typically used at three levels 
of design: 
1. Conceptual, for describing business entities as above 
2. Logical, for modeling the relationships and attributes of these entities in more detail 
3. Physical, to describe the mapping to database structures 
In the context of Business Architecture, conceptual and sometimes logical diagrams are the most 
useful, but will likely contain information types that have not been realized in business systems 
and databases. There is no restriction on key business information only including structures that 
have been, or even can be, reduced to structured data.

1.4 Key Business and Technical Drivers 
1.4.1 Problem Space: The Need for Boundaryless Information Flow 
The  Boundaryless  Information  Flow problem  space  is  one  that  is  shared  by  many  customer 
members of The Open Group, and by many similar organizations worldwide. It is essentially the

The  Boundaryless  Information  Flow problem  space  is  one  that  is  shared  by  many  customer 
members of The Open Group, and by many similar organizations worldwide. It is essentially the 
problem of getting information to the right people at the right time in a secure, reliable manner, 
in order to support the operations that are core to the extended enterprise. 
In General Electric, Jack Welch invented the term "the Boundaryless Organization", not to imply 
that there are no boundaries, but that they should be made permeable. 
Creating   organizational   structures   that   enabled   each   individual   department   to   operate   at 
maximum  efficiency  was  for  a  long  time  accepted  as  the  best  approach  to  managing  a  large 
enterprise.  Among  other  benefits,  this  approach fostered  the  development  of  specialist skills  in 
staff,  who  could  apply  those  skills  to  specific  aspects  of  an  overall  activity  (such  as  a

staff,  who  could  apply  those  skills  to  specific  aspects  of  an  overall  activity  (such  as  a 
manufacturing process), in order to accomplish the tasks involved better, faster, and cheaper. 
As  each  overall  activity  progressed  through  the  organization,  passing  from  department  to 
department  (for  example,  from  Design  to  Production  to  Sales),  each  department  would  take 
inputs  from  the  previous  department  in  the  process,  apply  its  own  business  processes  to  the 
activity, and send its output to the next department in line. 
In  today's  world  where  speed,  flexibility,  and responsiveness to changing  markets  make  all  the 
difference  between  success  and  failure,  this  method  of  working  is  no  longer  appropriate. 
Organizations have been trying for some time to overcome the limitations imposed by traditional 
organization structures. Many business process re-engineering efforts have been undertaken and

Organizations have been trying for some time to overcome the limitations imposed by traditional 
organization structures. Many business process re-engineering efforts have been undertaken and 
abandoned because they were too ambitious, while others cost far more in both time and money 
than originally intended. 
However, organizations today recognize  that they need  not abandon functional or departmental 
organization  altogether.  They  can  enable  the  right  people  to  come  together  in  cross-functional 
teams  so  that  all  the  skills,  knowledge,  and  expertise  can  be  brought  to  bear  on  any  specific 
problem or business opportunity. 
But this in turn poses its own challenges. CIOs are under enormous pressure to provide access to 
information  to  each  cross-functional  team  on  an  as-required  basis,  and  yet  the  sources  of  this 
data can be numerous and the volumes huge.

1.1 Overview 
As   the   market   environment   becomes   more   dynamic,   companies   are   moving   towards 
management  of  their  complexity  and  business  agility issues.  Networks  of  current  software 
components  and  their  interfaces  build  highly  complex  landscapes  where  change  management 
becomes  more  difficult  and  it is harder to  anticipate  and  comprehend  the  consequences  of 
change.  The  modern  market  environment  also  brings  demands  to  enhance  system  availability 
and scalability, two characteristics that are drivers in the adoption of MSA.

MSA  is  an architecture style that  defines  and  creates  systems  through  the  use  of  small 
independent and self-contained services that align closely with business activities. An individual 
microservice  is  a  service  that  is  implemented  with  a  single  purpose,  that  is  self-contained,  and

2 Microservices Architecture Defined 
Microservices  Architecture  (MSA) is  an  architecture  style,  in  which  software  systems  or 
applications  are  composed  of  one  or  more  independent  and self-contained  services.  It  is  not  a 
product,  framework,  or  platform.  It  is  a  strategy  for  building  large  distributed  systems. 
Microservices are loosely-coupled and deployed independently of one another. 
The  SOA  Source  Book (see Referenced  Documents) defines  a service  as  an  instantiation  of  a 
logical representation of a repeatable business activity that has a specified outcome. We define a 
microservice  as  a  self-contained  service  that  implements  an  Atomic Business  Function (ABF) 
and  is  independent  of  other  services.  MSA  is  a  style  of  architecture  that  defines  and  creates 
systems  through  the  use  of  small,  independent,  and  self-contained  services  that  closely  align

systems  through  the  use  of  small,  independent,  and  self-contained  services  that  closely  align 
with business activities. 
Microservices  are  the  primary  ABBs of  an  MSA.  An  MSA  has  the following  three  key 
characteristics: 
 Service-independence: each microservice is independent of other microservices; each 
microservice is developed, deployed, and changed independently 
 Single responsibility: each microservice is mapped to an atomic (single) business activity 
for which it is responsible 
 Self-containment: a microservice is a self-contained, independent deployable unit 
encompassing all external Information Technology (IT) resources (e.g., data sources, 
business rules) necessary to support the unique business activity

3.2 Implications for Business Architecture 
Business  Architecture has  a  pivotal  role  in the distributed  world.  In  addition  to  ensuring 
directional  alignment  with  enterprise  strategy,  it  takes  on  greater  responsibility  in  areas  of

are  often mapped  to  value  streams  that collapse  and  expand  the  existing  Business  Architecture 
design, and this has implications on organizational design and resources.

3.3 Implications for Data Architecture 
Distributed  architectures,  and  more  specifically MSAs,  introduce  more  copies  of  data  than 
centralized solutions. In order to meet certain non-functional requirements such as response time 
and availability targets, data may need to be copied to multiple data stores (e.g., operational data 
store  of  a  microservice,  cache,  edge  device)  so  that  the  lack  of  availability  and  latency  of 
upstream dependencies do not negatively impact the overall performance and availability of the 
microservice   and   ultimately   the   user   experience   of   the   applications   dependent   on   the 
microservice. Data  Architecture  and  governance  therefore  become   more  complex  as  the 
integration requirements, messaging, and analytic data related to these microservices evolve.

3.4 Implications for Application Architecture 
Monolithic  application  owners  have  the  luxury  of making  decisions  for  all  components  of  an

1.1 Overview 
As  the  business  environment  becomes  more  sophisticated,  the  challenges  facing  organizations 
are shifting away from questions of efficiency and automation towards questions of complexity 
management and business agility. 
Complex  webs  of  existing  applications  and  interfaces  create  highly  complex  landscapes  where 
change  becomes  more  and  more  difficult  and  the  impacts  of  change  become  harder  to  predict 
and understand. 
The concept of SOA provides an architectural style that is  specifically intended to simplify the 
business  and  the  interoperation  of  different  parts  of  that  business.  By  structuring  capability  as 
meaningful, granular services as opposed to opaque, silo’ed business units, it becomes possible 
to   quickly   identify   functional   capabilities   of   an   organization,   avoid   duplicating   similar 
capabilities across the organization, and quickly assemble new capabilities.

to   quickly   identify   functional   capabilities   of   an   organization,   avoid   duplicating   similar

By standardizing the behavior and interoperation of services, it is possible to limit the impacts of 
change and also to understand in advance the likely chain of impacts. 
From a software development perspective, SOA focuses on structuring applications in a way that 
facilitates  system  flexibility  and  agility – a  necessity  in  today’s  complex  and  fast-moving 
business environment.  SOA  aims  to  break  down  traditional  application  silos  into  portfolios  of 
granular  services  that  operate  in  open  and  interoperable  ways,  while  extracting  commodity 
capability into a virtualized infrastructure platform of shared re-usable utility services.

2 Service-Oriented Architecture Defined 
Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) is an architectural style that supports service-orientation. 
Service-orientation is a way of thinking in terms of services and service-based development and 
the outcomes of services. 
A  service  is  a  logical  representation  of  a  repeatable  business  activity  that  has  a  specified 
outcome  (e.g.,  check  customer  credit;  provide  weather  data,  consolidate  drilling  reports,  etc.) 
and: 
 Is self-contained 
 May be composed of other services 
 Is a “black box” to consumers of the service 
An  architectural  style is the  combination  of  distinctive  features  in  which  architecture  is 
performed or expressed.

1 Introduction 
Enterprise Architecture (including Security Architecture) is  all about aligning business systems 
and supporting information systems to realize business goals in an effective and efficient manner 
(systems  being  the  combination  of  processes,  people,  and  technology).  One  of  the  important 
quality  aspects  of  an  Enterprise  Architecture  is  information  security and  the  way  this  can  be 
managed. For  too long, information security has been considered  a  separate  discipline, isolated 
from the business processes and Enterprise Architecture. 
A  Security  Architecture is  a  structure  of  organizational,  conceptual,  logical,  and  physical 
components  that interact  in  a  coherent  fashion  in  order  to  achieve  and maintain  a  state  of 
managed  risk  and  security  (or  information  security). It  is both  a  driver  and  enabler  of  secure,

managed  risk  and  security  (or  information  security). It  is both  a  driver  and  enabler  of  secure, 
safe,  resilient, and reliable  behavior,  as  well  as  for  addressing risk  areas throughout  the 
enterprise. 
However,  an  Enterprise  Security  Architecture does  not  exist  in  isolation.  As  part  of  the 
enterprise,  it  builds on  enterprise  information  that  is  already  available  in  the  Enterprise 
Architecture,  and  it  produces  information  that  influences  the  Enterprise  Architecture.  This  is 
why  a  close integration of Security  Architecture  in the  Enterprise  Architecture  is  beneficial.  In 
the end, doing it right the first time saves costs and increases effectiveness compared to bolting

speak  the  same  language.  That  language  is  introduced  in  this  Guide,  which  describes  how  to

speak  the  same  language.  That  language  is  introduced  in  this  Guide,  which  describes  how  to 
integrate security and risk into an Enterprise Architecture. It provides guidance for both security
